why: A paid order started only as an in-memory background job, so every deploy or crash stranded paid orders until a later sweep refunded them. Every periodic job ran in every server process, a provider outage kept burning calls, nothing capped how much one customer could queue, the processing message always promised 20 to 30 seconds, and there was no way to run the server except by hand. A shop that grows past one phone and one laptop needs these fixed before it needs more customers.
approach: Paid orders, invoices and ops messages are written to a database 'outbox' first and picked up again after a restart; periodic jobs have a one-row lease so only one process runs each; providers have a circuit breaker, a rate smoother and a priority gate; a customer can have at most three paid orders in progress; the processing message uses measured times; middleware was made cheaper; uploads are size-checked as they stream; and Docker files describe how to run the stack. Everything is behind settings and needs no new service such as Redis.

decisions.decision: Use a database outbox (not Redis and Celery) to make paid orders survive restarts.
decisions.why: The database already exists and already holds the order state; the outbox is a table plus a sweep. It removes the 'lost on restart' risk now without the owner choosing and paying for a new service.

alternatives.why_not: Needs a hosting and Redis decision the owner has not made; kept as a later step if one server cannot cope.

alternatives.option: Keep in-memory background tasks and rely on the recovery sweep
alternatives.why_not: Orders are refunded after 10 minutes instead of being served.

decisions.decision: Run the order directly as before AND record it in the outbox first; the sweep only rescues orders nobody started after 90 seconds.
decisions.why: Customers see no change in speed, the server's shutdown still waits for orders in progress, and a crash can no longer lose an order.

alternatives.option: Let only the sweep run orders
alternatives.why_not: Adds up to 20 seconds of delay to every order.

decisions.decision: A per-provider circuit breaker with one probe after a cool-down, counting one failure per order (not per retry), and never counting refused prompts.
decisions.why: During an outage this makes orders fail fast and refund instead of waiting for several timeouts, while a blocked prompt (the customer's photo) is not the provider's fault.

alternatives.why_not: Two ordinary rate-limited orders would open the circuit.
Every order waits through the full timeout during an outage.

decisions.decision: Do not build photo-burst grouping (UX-1), object storage (DEP-3) or the full Celery queue yet.
decisions.why: Each needs a decision only the owner can make (how a batch is priced, which storage provider, whether to pay for Redis). They are recorded in docs/QUESTIONS_FOR_MORNING.md.

alternatives.why_not: Changes pricing and costs without their say.

errors.error: Reviewer: circuit breaker could stay open forever if the probe call was cancelled
errors.cause: The probe slot was only freed by a success, a failure or a neutral report; a cancelled probe reported nothing.
errors.fix: Every call chain now always reports an outcome (even on cancel or exception), and a probe that never reports expires after the cool-down.

errors.error: Reviewer: a re-delivered payment could send its invoice twice
errors.cause: 'Could not queue' and 'already queued' both looked like failure, so the code fell back to sending directly.
errors.fix: The outbox now says queued, duplicate or unavailable; a duplicate does nothing.

errors.error: TimeoutError: QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached (load scenario k)
errors.cause: The new queue-depth lookup used a second database connection while the request still held its own.
errors.fix: End the request's transaction before the lookup.

errors.error: Reviewer: in Docker every internet visitor shared one rate-limit bucket
errors.cause: uvicorn did not trust the proxy's forwarded address, so all traffic looked like it came from the proxy.
errors.fix: Start uvicorn with --proxy-headers and trust the private proxy network.
